doc.title: Mark Soskin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 17, 2021

title: Rollins's stage jump, following his solos, and his handwritten music
summary: Soskin recalls Rollins jumping off the stage and breaking his heel after quoting the Flying Trapeze, how the band joined in on his cues, and the Rollins handwritten charts and letters he now shows his students.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution

blocks.x: Well it’s so interesting. I had quite a number of Sonny Rollins records and I just yesterday watched a good deal of the video “Saxophone Colossus.”
That’s the one where he jumps off the —
Yes.
I was there.
And did you know he hurt himself?

Well what happened was that you know we’re playing and all of a sudden he jumps off the thing and we had no idea what was going on. And we were laughing. And then when we — at the end they said, “There’s not going to be an encore, we have to take Sonny away.” And he broke his heel.

I was fascinated by that, you know he’s doing his thing where he’s playing solo and in this one section he goes from “Give Me a Kiss to Build a Dream On” to something from the “Peer Gynt Suite” to the “The Flying Young Man” or the Flying Trapeze or whatever.
Right before he did that he quoted “The Man on the Flying Trapeze.”
Okay.
And that’s why that happened, and then he jumped.

So as a musician myself I sometimes wonder, I’m not sure that you or your bandmates at that time would have admitted it, but did you ever feel like, “Uh Mr. Rollins, we’ve been sitting here for a long time and we haven’t been playing anything, could we play now?”

Well I mean he was always playing, and we knew what to get into if he’d start something you know we’d get into it. Like if he started — whatever — “My One and Only Love” or something like that, we’d pick up on that.

Okay. So you were waiting — he’s doing his thing, he’s quoting these songs, and at some point he starts playing a song in a fashion that it’s your job, because you’ve been paying attention, now we join in.

That’s right. Yep. And you know I’m currently at — this is another thing — currently when I’m teaching now at Manhattan School of Music, which I started yesterday by the way, today I’m doing another class in improvisation. But when I was doing this yesterday this is the music of Sonny Rollins. This is the band. And I brought all the music because I still have all his music that I’ve kept and it’s in his handwriting. And the students just love that.
I’ll bet.
And we came up with a set list and now we’re getting into the tunes.
Awww. That’s awesome. I mean that’s pulling real life experience into the classroom which I think is so important.
Absolutely. Oh yeah. I mean look, we’re talking about Sonny Rollins. He’s like one of the last ones like this, alive. And you know, and to see the music in his handwriting, that’s something special.
Yeah. You hold on to that.

I am holding on to it. I have it right here. I have tons of it. You know and he’d send me the letters, you know letters that he wrote. I still have that too and I showed it to my students. And you know what can you say?
